title: Fannie Mae raises the condo reserve bar to 15% on January 4, 2027: what it means for selling or refinancing
seoTitle: Fannie Mae 15% Condo Reserves Jan. 2027: Florida Guide
description: From Jan. 4, 2027, Fannie Mae wants condo budgets to put 15% of assessment income into reserves. What changes for Florida buyers, sellers and boards.
dek: A Florida budget can follow state law and still make it hard for buyers in your building to get a conventional mortgage. Here is the new federal-market bar.
keywords: Fannie Mae condo limited review retired
facebook: Selling or refinancing a Florida condo next year? For Fannie Mae loans with applications from January 4, 2027, the building’s budget needs 15% going to reserves, up from 10%. What boards and owners should check now.

body.text: Most mortgages in America are bought by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac. When a buyer wants a conventional loan on a condo, the lender checks the whole building — its budget, its reserves, its insurance and its repairs — not just the unit. If the building doesn’t meet the rules, the building is called “non-warrantable,” and buyers usually need a different, often more expensive, kind of loan. In March 2026 Fannie Mae announced changes in Lender Letter LL-2026-03 that tighten those building rules.

Today a condo project generally needs to budget at least 10% of its assessment income for replacement reserves. For loan applications dated on or after January 4, 2027, that rises to 15%. The date that matters is when the buyer or refinancing owner applies for the loan, not when it closes. A project can meet the rule another way: by funding reserves at the highest level its reserve study recommends.

Here is the math in plain numbers. Say your association budgets $1,000,000 a year in owner assessments. Under the old 10% bar, $100,000 of that had to go to reserves. Under the new 15% bar, it is $150,000. In a 100-unit building that is $50,000 more a year, or about $42 more per unit per month, if the board gets there by raising assessments alone. Some buildings already clear 15% because their SIRS requires heavy reserves; others will not.

The same letter retired Fannie Mae’s “limited review,” a lighter check many lenders used for established buildings. For projects of more than 10 units, lenders now need a fuller review of the building’s documents. Fannie Mae also tightened what it accepts as a reserve study, and industry summaries report that a “baseline” funding plan — the minimum plan that keeps each reserve account just above zero — no longer counts toward its reserve-study option.

body.title: Why this matters in Florida
body.text: Florida’s SIRS rules require a baseline funding plan as a floor. A budget that satisfies Florida law at the floor can still fall short of Fannie Mae’s bar. The two systems measure different things.

items: Owners who want to sell: fewer buyers can use conventional financing in a non-warrantable building.
Owners who want to refinance: the same building review applies.
Boards: the reserve line in the 2027 budget now affects every owner’s ability to sell or borrow, not just the building’s repairs.

Board members: divide the 2027 reserve line by total budgeted assessment income. If it is under 15%, ask your manager and reserve professional what it would take to reach 15% or the highest recommended level in your study.
Owners planning to sell in 2027: ask the manager whether the building is expected to meet the new bar, and talk to a lender early.
Everyone: ask for the questionnaire answers your manager gives lenders — that is what buyers’ lenders see.

faq.q: What is the new Fannie Mae condo reserve requirement?
faq.a: For loan applications on or after January 4, 2027, a condo project must budget at least 15% of assessment income for reserves (up from 10%), or fund at the highest level its reserve study recommends.

faq.q: Does the date of the loan application or the closing matter?

faq.a: A condo project that does not meet Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac building standards, so buyers usually cannot get a standard conventional loan there.

faq.q: Is Fannie Mae’s limited review still available?
faq.a: Fannie Mae retired the limited review process in LL-2026-03; projects over 10 units now need a fuller review.
